title: Production & Factor Prices
text:
\[Y = A\,K^{\alpha} L^{1-\alpha}\]

\(A\) = total factor productivity, \(K\) = capital, \(L\) = labor, \(\alpha\) = capital’s share.
Marginal products: \(MPL = (1-\alpha)\dfrac{Y}{L}\),   \(MPK = \alpha\dfrac{Y}{K}\).
Factor prices: real wage \(W/P = MPL\); real rental \(R/P = MPK\).
Income shares are constant: labor gets \((1-\alpha)Y\), capital gets \(\alpha Y\) — they add up to \(Y\) (Euler).







Try it. Add capital and watch the wage rise but the rental rate fall. Change \(\alpha\) to re-slice the pie between labor and capital.





 
  Productivity A: 1.0
  Capital share α: 0.30
  Capital K: 125
  Labor L: 100
  
 
 






More capital → wage up, rental down (diminishing returns to capital).
More labor → wage down, rental up.
The shares (\(1-\alpha\) labor, \(\alpha\) capital) never change with K or L — only moving \(\alpha\) re-slices the pie.

title: How a Macro Model Works
text:
A model is a rule that turns exogenous variables (fed in from outside) into endogenous variables (solved inside).

Endogenous = determined by the model — here, the equilibrium price \(P\) and quantity \(Q\).
Exogenous = taken as given — here, buyers’ income and the input price.
Comparative statics = how the solution moves when an exogenous variable changes.




Demand slopes down: \(Q^d = 60 - 10P + 2\cdot\text{Income}\). Higher income shifts it right.
Supply slopes up: \(Q^s = 8P - 2\cdot\text{Input price}\). A costlier input shifts it left.
Equilibrium: the price where \(Q^d = Q^s\) — the market clears.







Try it. Raising income shifts demand right (P and Q both rise). Raising the input price shifts supply left (P rises, Q falls). The grey dot is the baseline.





 
  Buyers' income: 10
  
  Input price: 5
  
  
 
 







Income up → demand shifts right → both P and Q rise.
Input price up → supply shifts left → P rises, Q falls.
The model shows how a shock moves P and Q — not why income itself changed. That needs a bigger model.

title: Economic Fluctuations: AD / AS Shocks
text:
In the short run prices are sticky, so shocks move real output. In the long run prices adjust and output returns to its natural level. Three curves:

AD (aggregate demand): from \(M\cdot V = P\cdot Y\), so \(Y = \dfrac{M V}{P}\) — slopes down. Shifts right/left when M or V changes (a demand shock).
LRAS (long-run supply): vertical at natural output \(Y^*\) — output is pinned by K, L, technology, independent of prices.
SRAS (short-run supply): horizontal at the current (sticky) price level. A supply shock (oil, a bumper crop) shifts it up/down.




Demand shock (move AD): short run → output moves along the flat SRAS (price sticks); long run → SRAS adjusts, output returns to \(Y^*\), only the price level changes. The Fed can fully offset it.
Supply shock (shift SRAS): short run → output and prices move in opposite directions (adverse = stagflation); long run → the economy self-corrects back to \(Y^*\).







Try it. Move aggregate demand or hit a supply shock, then toggle Short run ↔︎ Long run to watch the economy adjust back to natural output. Loads instantly — plain JavaScript, no downloads.





 
  Aggregate demand  M·V  (demand shock): 10000
  
  Supply shock  (cost level): 0
  
  
    Short run
    Long run
  
  Reset to long-run equilibrium
  
 
 







Demand shock: move M·V only (leave supply at 0). In the short run output swings (boom/recession) while the price sticks. Flip to Long run — output snaps back to natural and only the price level has moved. That’s money neutrality, delayed.
Supply shock: slide Supply shock to adverse (+). In the short run output falls and prices rise together — stagflation. Flip to Long run — the economy self-corrects back to natural output and the shock unwinds.
The asymmetry: a demand shock can be fully offset by moving M·V back; a supply shock forces a choice between output and prices. Toggling short/long run shows why the two shocks feel so different.

title: The Costs of Inflation
text:
Shoeleather costs — effort to hold less cash when inflation is high.
Menu costs — the cost of changing posted prices.
Relative-price distortions — staggered price changes misallocate resources.
Redistribution (unexpected inflation) — fixed nominal contracts transfer wealth between borrowers and lenders.
Hyperinflation — all costs balloon; money stops working as a store of value.



A loan sets its nominal rate on expected inflation: \(i = r + \pi^e\). The lender’s realized real return is \(i - \pi\).

If actual \(\pi >\) expected → the borrower gains (repays in cheaper dollars).
If actual \(\pi <\) expected → the lender gains.







Try it. Fix the expected inflation the loan was priced on, then move actual inflation and watch who gains.





 
  Real rate the loan targets r (%): 2
  Expected inflation when signed pi_e (%): 3
  ACTUAL inflation pi (%): 3
  
 
 







Set actual = expected → ex post equals ex ante → no redistribution.
Push actual above expected → the lender’s realized return falls → borrower wins.
Menu, shoeleather, and relative-price costs happen even when inflation is fully expected; redistribution is the extra cost of the surprise.

title: Quantity Theory & Inflation
text:
The quantity equation is an identity: \(M \cdot V = P \cdot Y\).

\(M\) = money supply, \(V\) = velocity, \(P\) = price level, \(Y\) = real output.
In growth rates (writing \(\Delta\log X\) for the growth rate of \(X\)): \(\Delta\log M + \Delta\log V = \Delta\log P + \Delta\log Y\). With inflation \(\pi = \Delta\log P\),

\[\pi = \Delta\log M + \Delta\log V - \Delta\log Y\]

Quantity theory: if \(V\) is roughly constant (\(\Delta\log V \approx 0\)), then \(\pi = \Delta\log M - \Delta\log Y\) — sustained inflation comes from money growth outrunning real growth.
Classical dichotomy: in the long run money moves only nominal things (P), not real output.







Try it. Money growth above real growth → inflation. Faster output growth absorbs money and lowers inflation. Rising velocity adds to inflation.





 
  Money growth g_M (%): 5
  Output growth g_Y (%): 2
  Velocity growth g_V (%): 0
  
 
 






Set \(g_V = 0\): inflation is exactly \(g_M - g_Y\) — the pure quantity theory.
Faster output growth lowers inflation (more goods absorb the money).
Negative velocity growth pulls inflation down even if money grows.

title: The Fisher Effect & the Money Market
text:
Fisher equation: \(i = r + \pi^e\) — nominal rate = real rate + expected inflation.
Real money demand falls with \(i\). Here \((M/P)^d = \dfrac{Y}{2i}\).
Equilibrium: \(P\) adjusts so \(M/P = \dfrac{Y}{2i}\).
Velocity: \(V = \dfrac{PY}{M} = 2i\).
Ex ante real rate \(= i - \pi^e\); ex post \(= i - \pi\).







Try it. Raise expected inflation: \(i\) rises, people hold less real money, so \(P\) jumps more than the money stock. Watch velocity rise too.





 
  Money supply M: 1000
  Real rate r (%): 2
  Expected inflation pi_e (%): 3
  Real output Y: 1000
  
 
 






Defaults (M=1000, r=2, \(\pi^e\)=3, Y=1000) give i=5, P=10, V=10 — the exam short-answer baseline.
Raise \(\pi^e\): i and V rise, desired real balances fall, and P rises more than M.
The real rate r is set by the real economy; inflation just adds on top (Fisher).

title: The Solow Growth Model
text:
The classical model treats capital K and labor L as given: Y = F(K, L). It does not track how today’s saving becomes tomorrow’s capital. The Solow model adds that missing piece, a law of motion for capital, and uses it to answer three questions:

Why do economies with little capital grow fast, and why does that growth slow down (postwar Japan)?
Does saving more make a country grow faster forever, or only richer?
What is the only source of sustained growth in living standards?

title: The Solow Growth Model
text:
The classical model treats capital K and labor L as given: Y = F(K, L). It does not track how today’s saving becomes tomorrow’s capital. The Solow model adds that missing piece, a law of motion for capital, and uses it to answer three questions:

title: The Solow Growth Model
text:
The building blocks
Everything is measured per worker (lower-case letters), using constant returns to scale:








Piece
Equation
Meaning




Production
y = f(k)
Output per worker rises with capital per worker k = K/L, at a diminishing rate (MPK falls as k rises)


Saving = investment
i = s·y = s·f(k)
A fixed share s of output is saved and invested; c = (1 − s)·y is consumed


Depreciation
δ·k
Capital that wears out each period


Law of motion
Δk = s·f(k) − δ·k
Capital per worker grows when investment exceeds what is needed to replace worn-out capital


Steady state
s·f(k*) = δ·k*
Investment exactly covers break-even investment, so Δk = 0



With population growth n and labor-augmenting technology growth g, measure everything per effective worker (k̃ = K/(E·L)) and break-even investment becomes (δ + n + g)·k̃:

δ·k̃ replaces worn-out capital,
n·k̃ equips new workers,
g·k̃ keeps up with rising labor efficiency E.

These are the small-rate approximations used in the lecture (exact in continuous time).

text:
1. The Solow diagram






Try it. The defaults are the lecture’s numerical example: y = √k (α = 0.5), s = 0.30, δ = 0.10, n = g = 0, so k* = 9, y* = 3, c* = 2.1. Move one slider at a time and watch where the investment curve s·f(k) crosses the break-even line.






 
  Saving rate s:

  Population growth n: 
  
  Technology growth g: 
  
  Capital share α in y = kα: 
  
  
   Show Golden Rule
   Reset to lecture example
  
  
   f(k): output
   s·f(k): investment
   (δ+n+g)·k: break-even investment
  
  
 
 





What to notice

Saving (s up): the blue curve shifts up and k* moves right. Output per worker y* is permanently higher. That is a level effect.
Depreciation or population growth (δ or n up): the red line gets steeper and k* moves left. Faster population growth means lower output per worker, because each period’s investment is spread over more new workers (capital dilution).
Golden Rule: turn it on. Steady-state consumption c* = f(k*) − (δ+n+g)k* is largest where the slope of f(k) equals the slope of the break-even line: MPK = δ + n + g. With Cobb–Douglas output this happens exactly when s = α. In the lecture example, k*GR = 25, y*GR = 5, c*GR = 2.5 (above c* = 2.1 at s = 0.30).
The two extremes: at s = 1 everything is saved, so c = 0. At s = 0 nothing is invested, capital wears away, and since a worker with no capital produces nothing (f(0) = 0), output and consumption go to zero in the long run. Steady-state consumption is zero at both ends, so the best saving rate lies in between: the Golden Rule. (Try s = 0 in the table in section 3 below.)
Growth rates: whatever you do to s or n, long-run growth of Y/L is g. Only technology moves the long-run growth rate.

title: The Solow Growth Model
section: Why we need the Golden Rule
text:
Why we need the Golden Rule
The Solow diagram shows that saving more always raises steady-state capital and output. That raises a natural question: should a country just save as much as possible? No. People care about what they consume, not about how much capital or output exists. More saving builds capital but leaves a smaller share of output to consume (c = (1 − s) × y). We need a rule that picks the saving rate that is best for consumption in the long run. That rule is the Golden Rule: the saving rate that gives the most consumption per worker in the steady state.
Why such a rule must exist. Long-run consumption is zero at both extremes:

s = 1: everything is saved, so nothing is consumed.
s = 0: there is no investment, capital wears away, and output goes to zero (see the worked example in section 3).

Consumption is positive in between, so some saving rate in the middle gives the most. The Golden Rule finds it.
The condition. Steady-state consumption is c* = f(k*) − δk*. It is largest where one more unit of capital adds exactly as much output as it costs to maintain:

MPK = δ in the basic model.
MPK = δ + n + g once you add population growth and technology growth.

On the diagram, that is the point where the slope of f(k) equals the slope of the break-even line. Shortcut: with Cobb–Douglas output y = kα, the Golden Rule saving rate is just s = α.
Why it matters for policy. Comparing MPK with δ + n + g tells a country which way to move. Below the Golden Rule (MPK > δ + n + g) it should save more, which costs consumption today but raises it later. Above the Golden Rule (MPK < δ + n + g) it should save less, which raises consumption at every date. A high saving rate on its own does not tell you which case a country is in. Section 5 runs this check for the U.S.

What to notice

Level effect, not growth effect. Raise s from 0.30 to 0.40 and look at Growth rate of Y/L: growth jumps above g, then falls back to g. The economy ends up permanently richer but does not grow permanently faster.
Below the Golden Rule (old s < 0.50): switch to Consumption per worker. Consumption drops at period 10, then climbs above the old path. The current generation sacrifices for future ones.
Above the Golden Rule (try old s = 0.70, new s = 0.50): consumption jumps up immediately and stays above the old path at every date. Everyone gains.
Convergence. Growth is fastest right after the change, when k̃ is furthest below its new steady state. This is the model’s reading of postwar Japan.

title: The Solow Growth Model
text:
4. Growth accounting: the Solow residual
For Y = A·Kα·L1−α, output growth splits into capital, labor, and total factor productivity (TFP):
ΔY/Y ≈ α·ΔK/K + (1 − α)·ΔL/L + ΔA/A
TFP growth ΔA/A is what is left over: the Solow residual.

 
  Output growth ΔY/Y (%)
  Capital growth ΔK/K (%)
  Labor growth ΔL/L (%)
  Capital share α
 
 


The residual picks up everything not measured in K and L: genuine innovation, but also changes in capacity utilization, organization, reallocation across sectors, and measurement error.

title: The Solow Growth Model
text:
Convergence: conditional, not unconditional

Unconditional convergence (all poor countries grow faster than rich ones) is not what Solow predicts, and the cross-country data do not show it.
Conditional convergence: a country grows faster the further it starts below its own steady state. Countries with different saving, population growth, or technology have different steady states.
Low income alone does not imply fast growth. What matters is income relative to the country’s own long-run path.

title: The Solow Growth Model
text:
Check yourself


1. The saving rate permanently doubles from 20% to 40%. Does output per worker grow faster forever?

No. Growth of Y/L rises during the transition to the new, higher k*, then returns to g. The permanent effect is on the level of output per worker, not its growth rate.



2. Population growth n rises. What happens to k*, y*, and the growth rate of total output Y?

The break-even line (δ+n+g)k gets steeper, so k* and y* per worker fall (capital dilution). Total output Y grows faster in steady state, at n + g.



3. y = √k, δ = 0.10, n = g = 0. Find the Golden Rule capital stock and saving rate.

MPK = 0.5/√k = δ = 0.10, so √k = 5 and k*GR = 25. Then y = 5, break-even investment = 0.10 × 25 = 2.5, so s_GR = 2.5/5 = 0.5 (equal to α), and c*GR = 5 − 2.5 = 2.5.



4. An economy is above the Golden Rule. Should it save more or less, and who gains?

Less. Consumption jumps up immediately and stays higher along the whole transition, so every generation gains.



4b. A country saves nothing (s = 0). Why does its long-run consumption fall to zero even though it consumes all of its output?

With no investment, Δk = −δk: capital only depreciates and is never replaced, so k falls toward 0. Since f(0) = 0, output falls toward 0, and consumption (which equals output) falls with it. Steady-state consumption is f(0) − δ·0 = 0.



5. Output grows 3%, capital 4%, labor 1%, α = 0.3. What is TFP growth?

3 − 0.3(4) − 0.7(1) = 3 − 1.2 − 0.7 = 1.1%.



6. Two countries both have income per worker of $5,000. One grows at 5% a year, the other at 0.5%. Does this contradict the Solow model?

No. Each converges to its own steady state. The fast grower is likely far below its own k* (high saving, good institutions, technology adoption); the slow grower may already be near a low k*.



7. Which raises long-run living standards more: a permanent doubling of s, or a permanent 1-point rise in g?

The rise in g. Higher s gives a one-time level increase; higher g raises the growth rate of Y/L forever, so it eventually dominates any one-time level gain.

title: The Solow Growth Model
section: What the Solow model leaves unexplained
text:
What the Solow model leaves unexplained
The model takes s, n, and g as given. It does not explain where technological progress comes from, why saving rates differ across countries, or how human capital and institutions (compare North and South Korea) shape investment and innovation. It is also a real model: it says nothing about money, the price level, or inflation.

title: Large Open Economy & PPP
text:
A large economy’s saving and investment change the world interest rate. Two regions clear together: \(CA_H + CA_{ROW} = 0\), with each \(CA = S - I\) depending on \(r\).

A home fiscal expansion lowers home saving → pushes the world rate up → home investment falls (crowding out).
The adjustment is smaller than in a small economy, because the higher \(r\) pulls saving up and investment down everywhere.



The same good costs the same once converted: \(e = \dfrac{P_{\text{foreign}}}{P_{\text{home}}}\). Higher home inflation → the home currency depreciates one-for-one.






Try it. Left: a home fiscal expansion raises the world rate and crowds out investment. Right: a PPP calculator — change prices to get the exchange rate.





 
  Large open economy
  PPP calculator
 
 
  
   Home fiscal expansion (cuts saving): 0
  
  
   Home price of the good: 3
   Foreign price of the good: 6
  
  
 
 







Home fiscal expansion raises the world rate — unlike a small economy, where \(r^*\) is fixed.
Because \(r\) rises, home investment falls (crowding out).
In the PPP tab, raising the home price lowers \(e\) — the home currency buys less foreign currency.

title: Income Distribution & Inequality
text:
The skill premium is the wage ratio of skilled to unskilled workers, \(\omega = w_s/w_u\):
\[\omega = D \cdot \left(\frac{L_u}{L_s}\right)^{1/\sigma}\]

\(L_s/L_u\) = relative supply of skilled workers. More skilled workers (education) → \(\omega\) falls.
\(D\) = relative demand for skill. Skill-biased technical change (SBTC) raises \(D\) → \(\omega\) rises.
\(\sigma\) = how easily firms substitute the two types.







Try it. Educate more workers and the premium falls. Turn up SBTC and it rises — the race between education and technology.





 
  Skilled share of workers: 0.40
  Relative demand for skill D (SBTC): 1.5
  Substitutability σ: 2.0
  
 
 






Slide the skilled share up → the premium falls: expanding education compresses inequality.
Turn up SBTC (D) → the whole curve shifts up: technology favoring skill widens inequality.

title: Measuring the Economy
text:
GDP = market value of final goods produced: \(Y = C + I + G + NX\).
Nominal vs real: nominal GDP uses current prices; real GDP uses base-year prices (so it moves only when quantities move).
GDP deflator \(= \dfrac{\text{Nominal GDP}}{\text{Real GDP}}\times 100\) — a price index for everything the country produces.
Unemployment rate \(u = \dfrac{\text{Unemployed}}{\text{Labor force}}\);   LFPR \(= \dfrac{\text{Labor force}}{\text{Adult population}}\).







Try it. Change the quantity and current price to see nominal, real, and the deflator split apart. Then switch to the labor-market tab.





 
  GDP & the deflator
  Labor market
 
 
  
   One good. Base-year price fixed at $4.
   Quantity produced: 12
   Current price: 5
  
  
   Employed: 180
   Unemployed: 20
   Not in labor force: 50
  
  
 
 






Raise only the current price → nominal GDP rises, real GDP doesn’t → the deflator rises. That’s inflation.
Raise only the quantity → real GDP rises too.
In the labor tab, moving people to “not in labor force” lowers the LFPR but can lower measured unemployment — the denominators differ.

title: Loanable Funds & Crowding Out
text:
Think of all saving and borrowing in the economy as one market for a single good — loanable funds — whose “price” is the real interest rate \(r\).

Demand = investment \(I(r)\). Firms borrow to build capital; they borrow less when \(r\) is high, so demand slopes down.
Supply = national saving \(S\) = private \((Y-T-C)\) + public \((T-G)\) = \(Y - C - G\).
Equilibrium: \(r\) adjusts until saving equals investment, \(S = I(r)\).
Crowding out: a bigger deficit (raise \(G\), or cut \(T\)) lowers national saving → \(r\) rises → investment is squeezed.







Try it below. Push the government into deficit and watch \(r\) climb and investment fall. In the baseline, saving slopes up with \(r\); uncheck the box for the vertical-saving case.






  
    Government purchases G: 1500
    
    Taxes T: 1500
    
    Investment-demand shift: 0
    
     Saving slopes up (consumption responds to r) — uncheck for vertical saving
    
  
  
    
  







Run a deficit — raise \(G\) above \(T\). The saving line slides left, \(r\) climbs, and investment falls: crowding out, live.
Shift investment demand (baseline, saving slopes up): \(r\) rises and investment rises.
Uncheck the box for vertical saving and shift demand again: \(r\) rises but \(I^*\) stays put. This is the difference between the two exam cases.

title: Small Open Economy & the Exchange Rate
text:
With perfect capital mobility, a small country takes the world interest rate as given: \(r = r^*\).

Net exports = net capital outflow: \(NX = S - I = NFI\).
\(r^*\) fixes investment \(I(r^*)\), so it fixes \(S - I\) — hence the trade balance.
The real exchange rate \(\varepsilon\) adjusts so \(NX(\varepsilon) = S - I\).
Tariff: doesn’t touch \(S\) or \(I\) → \(S-I\) fixed → shifts \(NX(\varepsilon)\), so \(\varepsilon\) appreciates but NX is unchanged.







Try it. Left panel: \(r^*\) fixes investment; the gap to saving is net capital outflow. Right panel: the exchange rate slides so net exports equal that gap. A tariff moves \(\varepsilon\) but not NX.





 
  Government purchases G: 1500
  Taxes T: 1500
  Investment-demand shift: 0
  World rate r* (%): 5
  Import tariff (shifts NX): 0
  
 
 






Deficit (G above T): saving slides left, NFI falls, \(\varepsilon\) appreciates.
Lower \(r^*\): investment rises, NFI falls, currency appreciates, NX falls.
Tariff: only the right panel’s NX curve shifts — \(\varepsilon\) rises but the trade balance (NFI) is unchanged. Protectionism can’t fix a trade deficit.

title: What Is Money?
text:
Money = the stock of assets you own and can spend now. It does three jobs: medium of exchange, store of value, unit of account.

Fiat money (dollars) has no intrinsic value; commodity money (gold) does.
Aggregates by liquidity: M0 (currency + reserves) ⊂ M1 (+ checking) ⊂ M2 (+ savings).
Banks lend out deposits, so the base multiplies:

\[M = B \cdot \frac{1+c}{rr+c}\]
\(B\) = monetary base, \(rr\) = reserve ratio, \(c\) = currency-to-deposit ratio. The fraction is the money multiplier.






Try it. An open-market purchase raises the base \(B\). A lower reserve ratio raises the multiplier. Both expand the money supply.





 
  Monetary base B (open-market ops): 500
  Reserve ratio rr: 0.10
  Currency/deposit ratio c: 0.20
  
 
 






A credit-card limit, a check in transit, and an unused credit line are not money — only owned, spendable balances count.
Lower reserve ratio → bigger multiplier → more money from the same base.
The Fed buys bonds to raise B (expand), sells to shrink it.
